input_signals.name: PersistentExternallyFundedExpansion
input_signals.expression: MUL(TS_SUM(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), at), 3), TS_SUM(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(prstkc, dltr)), at), 1), 3))
input_signals.hypothesis: Multi-year investment programs continuously refinanced by external capital markets reflect entrenched empire building, whereas a single year of externally funded capex can be lumpy but value-creating.
input_signals.reasoning: The product of a three-year cumulative investment rate and a three-year cumulative net external financing rate is large only for firms that repeatedly spend and repeatedly raise, capturing a persistent state rather than a one-off transaction. Smoothing both legs also reduces the annual-report noise that weakens contemporaneous interaction sorts.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ts_sum( ratio( add( capx, aqc ), at ), 3 ), ts_sum( winsor( ratio( sub( add( sstk, dltis ), add( prstkc, dltr ) ), at ), 1 ), 3 ) )

input_signals.name: IssuanceInvestmentMismatch
input_signals.expression: SUB(IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)), IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Capital raised in excess of what the firm actually deploys into investment is the purest evidence of opportunistic market timing; matched issuance-and-investment is much less informative because the money has an identified use.
input_signals.reasoning: Differencing industry ranks of gross external issuance and gross investment isolates the wedge between funds raised and funds spent, so the extreme short leg contains issuers with no corresponding real spending. It is a mismatch (orthogonalized) interaction rather than a product, and therefore captures a distinct part of the investment-financing joint distribution from Signals 1-4.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( ind_rank( ratio( add( sstk, dltis ), at ) ), ind_rank( ratio( add( capx, aqc ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: StockSwapIntangibleExpansion
input_signals.hypothesis: Deals paid for with the firm's own paper leave a balance-sheet footprint (a jump in goodwill and other intangibles plus a jump in shares outstanding) without a matching cash outflow, and this paper-funded expansion signals managerial belief that the equity is overvalued.
input_signals.reasoning: This fixes the measurement error the critic identified: cash-acquisition spend (aqc) is dropped entirely and deal activity is measured by the growth in total intangibles, which rises for stock-swap deals precisely because no cash leaves the firm. The consideration channel is proxied by two complementary issuance measures combined with SUMRANK, so a share count inflated by a split (which does not raise sstk) or an equity raise held as cash (which does not grow intangibles) cannot by itself place a firm in the short leg; both legs are non-negative ranks, so the score is monotone.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( delta( intan, 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ), sumrank( ratio( sstk, at ), winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: LeveredCapacityBuild
input_signals.hypothesis: Gross capacity added with newly borrowed money creates committed fixed costs and inflexible, hard-to-reverse assets, so these firms underperform once the capacity fails to earn its cost of capital; identical capacity growth funded without new debt carries no such burden.
input_signals.reasoning: Ranking PP&E growth before multiplying removes the sign flip the critic flagged: shrinking-asset borrowers now receive a low PP&E-growth rank and therefore a low, not extreme-negative, score, so they no longer populate the leg that is supposed to hold conservative firms. Both inputs are non-negative industry ranks, so the score rises monotonically in capacity growth and in *net* debt raised (issuance minus retirement, rather than the change in debt balances, which mixes in reclassification and currency effects), and the short leg is unambiguously the levered capacity builder.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( growth( ppegt, 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ratio( sub( dltis, dltr ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: NonCashDealExpansion
input_signals.hypothesis: Intangible and goodwill growth that is *not* matched by cash acquisition outlays must have been paid for in paper, and paper-funded expansion signals that management is exploiting an overvalued equity price.
input_signals.reasoning: This sharpens the batch's best portfolio performer by subtracting cash acquisition spend from intangible growth, so the investment leg now measures the specifically non-cash-funded part of deal-driven expansion rather than all intangible growth. The consideration leg switches from sstk to share-count growth, which is available for nearly every firm-year, addressing the low coverage that made the original's deciles thin.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( sub( delta( intan, 1 ), aqc ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: IssuedAndSpentVersusHoarded
input_signals.hypothesis: New equity that is immediately converted into physical investment reveals overinvestment, whereas new equity parked in cash is a precautionary buffer that carries no such penalty and may even predict higher returns.
input_signals.reasoning: This directly confronts the critic's Palazzo objection to the accepted mismatch signal by separating the deployment of raised capital from its retention: the second factor is positive only when issuance exceeds cash accumulation, so the interaction shorts high-capex issuers who spent the money and goes long high-capex firms building cash without issuing. It tests whether the pricing consequence of external financing depends on where the money went, a conditioning dimension no prior proposal in the archive addresses.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( capx, lag( ppent, 1 ) ), 1 ) ), sub( ind_rank( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ratio( delta( che, 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: CapexFundingMixTilt
input_signals.hypothesis: For a given rate of capital spending, the source of the money is what predicts returns: each dollar of capex backed by newly raised outside claims reflects an expansion the firm could not fund itself, whereas capex covered by internal resources is a positive signal.
input_signals.reasoning: The financing leg is now a funding *mix* — liability dollars raised per dollar of capital spending, industry-demeaned and signed — rather than a level of debt growth, so scaling investment and financing up together leaves the score unchanged and the construct cannot be a restatement of asset growth or of the debt-issuance anomaly. The non-negative capex-rate rank acts purely as an exposure weight: low investors score near zero regardless of funding mix, while heavy investors are sorted by whether the program was outside-funded (short leg) or self-funded (long leg), which is the interaction the theme asks for.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( capx, lag( ppegt, 1 ) ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( delta( lt, 1 ), capx ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: TradeCreditFundedInventory
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(invt, 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(SUB(lt, dltt), 1), DELTA(che, 1)), LAG(at, 1)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Inventory accumulation is benign when the firm pays for it out of its own cash, but signals unsold goods plus a liquidity squeeze when it is carried on payables and short-term credit while cash is not drawn down.
input_signals.reasoning: The financing leg is rebuilt as total liabilities less long-term debt, which is genuinely current liabilities including payables — this both removes the Δdlc double count the critic identified and delivers the trade-credit content the hypothesis claimed. Adding the change in cash makes the leg a funding-source contrast rather than a growth level: it is high only when short-term outside claims expand *without* internal cash being spent, and because that leg is signed and industry-demeaned the product separates externally financed inventory builds (short) from self-funded ones (long) instead of collapsing onto inventory or asset growth.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( delta( invt, 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( add( delta( sub( lt, dltt ), 1 ), delta( che, 1 ) ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: DealDeploymentVersusHoarding
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(aqc, DELTA(intan, 1)), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(che, 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The overvaluation content of external financing depends on whether the money is converted into acquired businesses and intangibles or retained as cash; deal-driven external growth is the empire-building case, cash retention is precautionary.
input_signals.reasoning: This holds the winning conditioning structure fixed and swaps the investment channel from organic capex to inorganic expansion (cash acquisitions plus intangible additions), which is the cleanest way to learn whether the deploy-versus-hoard dimension is a general funding-source effect or specific to capital spending. It also directly reuses the diagnostic that intangible/deal growth interacted with issuance gave the strongest FMB slopes in the archive but no aligned portfolio alpha when built as a non-negative rank product.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( add( aqc, delta( intan, 1 ) ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ), sub( ind_rank( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ratio( delta( che, 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: PeakInvestmentOnOutsideMoney
input_signals.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1), 5), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(GROWTH(csho, 1), RATIO(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), LAG(at, 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters is not whether a firm invests a lot relative to peers but whether it is at the top of its own investment cycle while leaning on capital markets — cyclical peak spending financed externally is where extrapolative overinvestment concentrates.
input_signals.reasoning: TS_RANK places the current capex rate in the firm's own five-year history, removing the cross-sectional capex-intensity level that plausibly drives most of the FF5 alpha in the two archive signals sharing a capex leg, so a result here would be genuinely incremental to the investment main effect. The financing leg is an industry-demeaned signed combination of share-count growth and debt growth, so peak investors funding internally take the opposite tail rather than clustering at zero.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ts_rank( winsor( ratio( capx, lag( ppent, 1 ) ), 1 ), 5 ), ind_zscore( sumrank( growth( csho, 1 ), ratio( delta( add( dltt, dlc ), 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: DeployingLastYearsRaise
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(LAG(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1), LAG(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Capital is raised before it is spent, and the mispricing is resolved during the deployment stage: firms that ramp up capital spending this year using money raised from markets last year are the ones whose expansion plans were validated only by cheap external capital, not by internal cash generation.
input_signals.reasoning: The mechanism is the sequencing of the funding cycle rather than the contemporaneous funding mix, so the investment leg is the *change* in the capex rate (the ramp) and the financing leg is prior-year external funding, a combination no archive signal contains and which cannot be a reparameterization of PayoutFundedInvestment or the mismatch family. The financing leg is industry-demeaned and signed, so firms ramping investment without a prior raise take the opposite tail, and the lag structure also means the signal is measured after issuance-window effects have largely passed.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( delta( ratio( capx, lag( ppent, 1 ) ), 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( sumrank( lag( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ), lag( ratio( delta( add( dltt, dlc ), 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: FundedInvestmentRampVersusOwnNorm
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), MA(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 3)), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(che, 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Overinvestment shows up as a firm spending abnormally relative to its own recent norm while simultaneously spending fresh outside capital; a firm at its usual investment rate, or one that banked the money it raised, has not overextended.
input_signals.reasoning: PeakInvestmentOnOutsideMoney had the strongest FMB slope in the archive (-4.76) but no alpha, and its two suspects are a five-valued TS_RANK weight and a z-score financing leg; this replaces the first with a continuous deviation from the firm's own three-year average capex rate and the second with the deploy-versus-hoard rank contrast that has demonstrated portfolio traction. If it works, it shows the within-firm timing insight was real and only the portfolio construction was broken, which is a genuinely diagnostic outcome.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( sub( ratio( capx, lag( ppent, 1 ) ), ma( ratio( capx, lag( ppent, 1 ) ), 3 ) ), 1 ) ), sub( ind_rank( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ratio( delta( che, 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: UnstablyFundedInvestment
input_signals.hypothesis: Long-lived investment programs financed by an erratic, stop-start stream of equity issuance are fragile — the firm cannot commit to completing them — whereas the same programs financed by the steady internal cash flow evidenced by a stable dividend are sustainable.
input_signals.reasoning: Every archive signal characterizes funding by its level or sign; none uses the *second moment* of the funding stream, yet financing volatility is precisely what distinguishes an opportunistic serial issuer from a firm with a reliable funding plan. The contrast subtracts a smoothed dividend rate so the long tail is heavy investors with steady internal funding and the short tail is heavy investors with volatile market funding, keeping the sort two-tailed within the high-investment group.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( capx, lag( ppent, 1 ) ), 1 ) ), sub( ind_rank( vol( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ), 5 ) ), ind_rank( ma( ratio( dvc, at ), 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: PeckingOrderViolationInvestment
input_signals.hypothesis: A heavy investor that issues equity while its balance sheet still has ample unused debt capacity is violating the pecking order, and the only coherent reason to prefer expensive equity over cheap debt is that management thinks the shares are overpriced; a heavy investor that is already highly levered issues equity out of necessity, not opportunism.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic is right that differencing two same-signed anomalies is unmotivated, so the debt leg is replaced by the *level* of leverage, which theory and evidence associate with higher — not lower — expected returns, meaning the long tail (levered, non-issuing investors) is no longer stacked with a known negative predictor. The score therefore identifies the specific pecking-order violation that reveals market timing, and both tails remain heavy investors so the sort is a funding-choice comparison rather than an investment-intensity sort.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( capx, lag( ppent, 1 ) ), 1 ) ), sub( ind_rank( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ratio( lt, at ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ForcedIssuanceAtLiquidityTrough
input_signals.hypothesis: Issuing equity when the firm's own liquidity has fallen to the bottom of its five-year range is forced financing on the market's terms, while issuing from the top of its liquidity range is opportunistic and discretionary; only the forced case reveals that the investment program has outrun the firm's capacity to fund it.
input_signals.reasoning: Cross-sectional cash levels conflate industry norms and business models, whereas the firm's position within its own liquidity history measures whether the buffer is genuinely depleted — the same within-firm reframing that turned a flat-alpha signal into a working one in gen 3. Both legs are bounded in [0,1] so the contrast is well scaled, and heavy investors at their liquidity peak occupy the long tail rather than being pooled at zero.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( capx, lag( ppent, 1 ) ), 1 ) ), sub( ind_rank( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ), ts_rank( ratio( che, at ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: WorkingCapitalReleaseFundedRamp
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm that steps up capital spending by squeezing cash out of its own working capital is reallocating internally under operating discipline, whereas a firm that funds the identical step-up by issuing shares has bought growth with other people's money; the first expansion is validated by the business, the second only by the share price.
input_signals.reasoning: Working capital has appeared in the archive only as a *use* of funds (TradeCreditFundedInventory); treating inventory liquidation as a *source* of funds for an investment ramp is a new economic channel and the only internal funding source that is observable without any income-statement input. The contrast is signed and both tails are firms ramping investment, so the sort compares two funding routes for the same real action rather than restating the inventory-growth or issuance main effects.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( delta( ratio( capx, lag( ppent, 1 ) ), 1 ), 1 ) ), sub( ind_rank( winsor( neg( ratio( delta( invt, 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: SelfFundedVersusMarketFundedGate
input_signals.hypothesis: The identical investment rate carries opposite information depending on the funding regime: for a firm that returns more cash to shareholders than it takes from them, heavy investment signals profitable opportunities, while for a firm that is a net taker of shareholder capital the same heavy investment signals overvaluation-driven expansion.
input_signals.reasoning: This uses a hard sign gate rather than a graded rank difference, which is a structurally different conditioning device from anything in the archive: the score is +capex-rank for net-payer firms and −capex-rank for net-taker firms, so both extreme deciles are heavy investors and the spread is a pure funding-regime contrast with the investment main effect differenced out. The direction is supported independently of any single prior result — PayoutFundedInvestment (fmb +1.84, alpha +1.7%) and IssuedAndSpentVersusHoarded (alpha -2.5% for the spending issuers) both point to payers being the good side within high investors.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( capx, lag( ppent, 1 ) ), 1 ) ), sign( sub( ind_rank( ratio( dvc, at ) ), ind_rank( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: FinancingChurnInvestor
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1)), MIN(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(dvc, prstkc), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm that takes capital from shareholders and simultaneously hands capital back while investing heavily has no coherent funding plan; this churn is a symptom of managers who will not subordinate distributions to their own investment program, and it signals weak capital discipline rather than either genuine self-funding or clean market funding.
input_signals.reasoning: Every archive construction treats raising and returning capital as opposite poles of one axis, so the case where both are large simultaneously has never been isolated; MIN is the natural operator for "both at once" and has not been used in any prior entry. The high tail is heavy investors who are round-tripping shareholder capital, the low tail is heavy investors doing neither, so the score is orthogonal by construction to the net-financing measures that dominate the archive.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( capx, lag( ppent, 1 ) ), 1 ) ), min( ind_rank( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( ratio( add( dvc, prstkc ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: YoungBaseExternallyFundedExpansion
input_signals.hypothesis: Externally funded investment is defensible when it replaces a worn-out asset base and suspicious when the existing base is already new: a firm whose plant is largely undepreciated yet keeps raising shareholder capital instead of distributing it is adding capacity the business does not need to maintain.
input_signals.reasoning: The ratio of net to gross PP&E is a clean vintage measure that separates replacement investment from genuine expansion, a distinction the archive has never made even though it is central to whether spending is value-neutral maintenance or discretionary empire building. Because the vintage weight is a level and the funding leg is a signed issuance-versus-payout contrast, both tails are young-asset-base firms and the sort cannot restate the investment-growth or issuance main effects.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( ppent, ppegt ), 1 ) ), sub( ind_rank( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( ratio( dvc, at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: DilutionWithoutCapitalAccumulation
input_signals.hypothesis: Issuing shares while the equity cushion per unit of assets is shrinking means the new capital is being consumed as fast as it arrives, so existing owners are diluted without the firm's capital base growing; a heavy investor whose equity share of assets is rising without dilution is funding itself out of retained value.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the financing-deficit identity the critic correctly identified as net external financing and instead measures whether shareholder dilution is accompanied by any accumulation of the equity claim, a stock-versus-flow inconsistency that no archive entry examines and that is not the issuance anomaly (issuers whose equity ratio climbs land in the opposite tail). Both tails are heavy investors, so the sort prices how the expansion was capitalized rather than the level of investment or of issuance.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( capx, lag( ppent, 1 ) ), 1 ) ), sub( ind_rank( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( winsor( delta( ratio( ceq, at ), 1 ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: CollateralPoorDependence
input_signals.hypothesis: Market dependence bites hardest where the asset base cannot be pledged: an intangible-heavy firm that is issuing equity from a thin cash position has no collateral to fall back on if capital markets close, whereas a tangible-asset firm in the same funding position retains borrowing capacity.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive has weighted the funding-versus-liquidity contrast by investment intensity, deal intensity, asset vintage and issuance, but never by asset *pledgeability*, which is the variable that determines whether external dependence is a real constraint or a choice. Both tails are intangible-heavy firms, so the sort prices funding fragility conditional on collateral rather than restating the intangible-intensity or issuance effects.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( intan, at ), 1 ) ), sub( ind_rank( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ratio( che, lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: RealizedVersusLatentDependence
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), ADD(ADD(capx, aqc), ADD(che, ADD(dvc, prstkc)))), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sstk, prstkc), LAG(at, 1)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Having an investment program that exceeds internal resources is only a warning if the firm actually acted on it: a structurally dependent firm that went to shareholders for net new capital has confirmed the gap, while an equally dependent firm that instead bought back stock must have had funding capacity the balance sheet does not show.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the level-plus-momentum construction the critic objected to with a latent-versus-realized distinction: the bounded uncovered-share measure identifies who *needs* outside money and the signed net equity flow identifies who *took* it, so the interaction separates confirmed dependence from apparent dependence. Because the financing leg is signed and centred, dependent repurchasers occupy the long tail and non-dependent firms cluster near zero regardless of their issuance, which keeps the sort focused on the interaction rather than on the issuance main effect.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( add( capx, aqc ), add( add( capx, aqc ), add( che, add( dvc, prstkc ) ) ) ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( sstk, prstkc ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: OutsideFundingBreadthCapex
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppent, 1)), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), 1), LAG(at, 1)), GROWTH(csho, 1))), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(che, LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Non-interest-bearing operating credit and new equity are both outside money that a capital-spending firm can lean on, and a firm funding its program from either while holding no liquid buffer is dependent regardless of which of the two it used.
input_signals.reasoning: SupplierFundedCapex delivered a strong alpha (-3.1%, t -3.35) but a weak slope (-1.57), and the natural diagnosis is that operating-liability growth alone is a narrow, noisy funding channel; pooling it with equity issuance broadens the funding leg without abandoning the supplier-credit insight. This also partially addresses the critic's concern that the leg is a pure operating-liability sort, since a firm scoring high must be short of cash while funded from at least one outside source.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( capx, lag( ppent, 1 ) ), 1 ) ), sub( ind_rank( sumrank( ratio( delta( sub( lt, add( dltt, dlc ) ), 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ), growth( csho, 1 ) ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ratio( che, lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ChronicDependenceCount
input_signals.expression: TS_SUM(MIN(INDICATOR(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1), 0.02), INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), LAG(at, 1)), RATIO(che, LAG(at, 1))), 0)), 3)
input_signals.hypothesis: Being externally dependent for one year can be a lumpy project; being dependent for three years running is a business model, and chronic dependence identifies firms whose expansion has never been validated by internally generated resources.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive measures the dependent state only contemporaneously; this counts how many of the last three years the firm was simultaneously issuing equity and running an investment program larger than its cash balance, using MIN as a logical AND on the two indicators. It is a discrete, slow-moving state variable, which should give far more stable portfolio composition than the annual-flow constructions whose deciles turn over every year, and its long tail is firms that have never been in the dependent state.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ts_sum( min( indicator( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ), 0.02 ), indicator( sub( ratio( add( capx, aqc ), lag( at, 1 ) ), ratio( che, lag( at, 1 ) ) ), 0 ) ), 3 )

input_signals.name: BorrowingHeadroomDependence
input_signals.hypothesis: What makes market dependence bite is having no debt capacity left: a firm whose pledgeable plant is small relative to the claims already outstanding cannot borrow if equity markets close, so cash-poor equity issuance by such a firm is genuinely forced, whereas a firm with plant far exceeding its liabilities always retains a secured-borrowing fallback.
input_signals.reasoning: The weight is now collateral measured against existing claims rather than asset composition, so it excludes cash entirely and is not contaminated by the liquidity the contrast leg subtracts — it is itself a cross-theme quantity (pledgeable investment assets versus total financing claims) and is economically distinct from the intangible-intensity predictor. It also has full continuous support across the cross-section, which the archive shows is the condition under which this architecture produces a cross-sectional slope as well as an alpha.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( neg( ratio( ppent, lt ) ), 1 ) ), sub( ind_rank( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ratio( che, lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ErraticProgramDependence
input_signals.hypothesis: Outside investors cannot discipline a spending program they cannot predict: firms whose investment rate swings wildly from year to year give suppliers of capital no benchmark, so when such a firm funds itself with equity from a thin cash position the money is most likely to be misallocated, while a steady-state investor's external funding is verifiable against a stable plan.
input_signals.reasoning: Every conditioning weight tried so far is a level or a composition measure; this one is the second moment of the *investment* program, which is a different economic quantity from the financing volatility tested earlier (UnstablyFundedInvestment, which measured issuance instability and gave a wrong-signed alpha). It has broad continuous support by construction, and it identifies the population where monitoring is hardest rather than merely restating who invests or who issues.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( vol( winsor( ratio( capx, lag( ppent, 1 ) ), 1 ), 5 ) ), sub( ind_rank( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ratio( che, lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: TotalFundingCapacityGap
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(che, ppent), lt), at), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm's true internal funding capacity is its liquid balance plus what its pledgeable assets can support net of the claims already against them; issuing equity while that whole capacity is thin is the state that reveals dependence, whereas issuing while capacity is ample is discretionary.
input_signals.reasoning: Rather than adding payout flows to a cash stock — the dimensionally sloppy change the critic rejected — this replaces the resource leg with a single stock-consistent measure of net pledgeable liquidity (cash plus plant less total liabilities), which brings debt capacity into the definition of internal resources for the first time in this archive. The investment-intensity weight is retained unchanged so the comparison against the existing cash-only formulation is clean, and both tails remain heavy investors.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( add( capx, aqc ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ), sub( ind_rank( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ratio( sub( add( che, ppent ), lt ), at ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: PeakProgramFundingGap
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), LAG(at, 1)), TS_MAX(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), LAG(at, 1)), 5)), 1), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(che, LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Externally funded expansion is most dangerous at the top of a firm's own spending cycle, when commitments are maximal and reversal is costly; a firm running its largest program in five years on outside money from an empty balance sheet is at maximum overextension, while the same funding position at the bottom of its own cycle carries little commitment.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the positive-side self-funding construction the critic correctly noted has already failed twice and instead supplies the one weight the archive has evidence for but never implemented continuously — within-firm cycle position, which produced the strongest FMB slopes when coarsely proxied by TS_RANK and MA deviations. Expressing it as the ratio of the current program to the firm's own five-year maximum gives a bounded, continuous, firm-demeaned weight that cannot be a restatement of the cross-sectional investment level, paired with the contrast that reliably carries the FF5 alpha.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ratio( ratio( add( capx, aqc ), lag( at, 1 ) ), ts_max( ratio( add( capx, aqc ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 5 ) ), 1 ), sub( ind_rank( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ratio( che, lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: CollateralErosionDependence
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm whose tangible base is actively shrinking while it raises equity from an empty balance sheet is substituting outside capital for collateral it is losing; the direction of collateral change, not just its level, tells us whether the funding position is deteriorating.
input_signals.reasoning: Every conditioner tested so far is a level or a second moment; this is the first-difference version, which identifies firms whose secured-borrowing capacity is being eroded in real time — a state that the level-based headroom measure cannot see in firms that still look asset-rich. It is economically distinct from asset-growth sorts because the score is high only when shrinking collateral coincides with cash-poor issuance, and low for shrinking firms that are liquid or repurchasing.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( neg( ratio( delta( ppent, 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ), 1 ) ), sub( ind_rank( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ratio( che, lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: PledgeabilityWithoutLeverage
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(ppent, SUB(at, che))), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(che, LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: What conditions the penalty for cash-poor equity funding is the physical pledgeability of the operating asset base, not how indebted the firm already is; a firm whose non-cash assets are mostly unpledgeable has no secured fallback regardless of its current leverage.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic's observation that NEG(ppent/lt) rises mechanically with total liabilities is important economically, not just cosmetically: the champion's -4.6% alpha may be a leverage-distress effect rather than a collateral effect. Scaling plant by non-cash assets purges liabilities from the weight entirely and also removes cash from the denominator, so this is a decomposition test whose outcome tells us which of two very different mechanisms the archive's best result rests on, and it keeps the champion's coverage.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( neg( ratio( ppent, sub( at, che ) ) ), 1 ) ), sub( ind_rank( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ratio( che, lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: NearTermCashRequirementCoverage
input_signals.expression: IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(ADD(capx, aqc), ADD(dlc, dvc)), ADD(che, ppent)), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm's total call on cash over the coming year is its investment program plus the debt maturing plus the dividend it is expected to keep paying, and the resources it can meet that call with internally are its cash balance and the plant it could pledge or sell; when the call exceeds those resources the firm must go to the market on whatever terms are available.
input_signals.reasoning: This drops the weight-times-contrast architecture entirely in favour of a single coverage ratio, which removes the leverage double-count the critic identified — liabilities now appear once, in the numerator, and never in the conditioner — and eliminates the dispersion compression that multiplicative weights impose. It is also the only construction in the archive that puts investment, maturing debt and the payout commitment on the same side of a resource comparison, and its denominator uses pledgeable plant rather than cash alone, so it is not a restatement of any tested entry.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( add( add( capx, aqc ), add( dlc, dvc ) ), add( che, ppent ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: IrreversibleProgramDependence
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, ADD(capx, ADD(aqc, ABS(DELTA(invt, 1))))), 1)), SUB(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(che, LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Externally funded expansion is most damaging when the money is sunk into assets the firm cannot walk away from: a program concentrated in fixed plant cannot be scaled back if funding dries up, whereas spending on acquisitions or inventory can be resold or run down, so irreversibility determines whether market dependence becomes a trap.
input_signals.reasoning: Rather than stacking two conditioners that have already been evaluated, this introduces a conditioner the archive has never used — the composition of the investment program between irreversible plant and reversible outlays — which is the standard real-options determinant of why overinvestment destroys value. The weight is a bounded composition share with broad support and no overlap with collateral, vintage, volatility or cycle position, so a result here is attributable to irreversibility rather than to a repackaging of the champion's weight.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( capx, add( capx, add( aqc, abs( delta( invt, 1 ) ) ) ) ), 1 ) ), sub( ind_rank( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ratio( che, lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: CoverageDeterioration
input_signals.hypothesis: What predicts returns is not only how dependent a firm is but whether it is becoming more so: a year in which cash requirements grew relative to internal resources marks the point at which management committed beyond its means, regardless of the starting level.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive has established the level of funding coverage as a powerful state variable but has never tested its first difference in a stable functional form, and the log difference is a clean growth-rate of the dependence state that is orthogonal by construction to the cross-sectional level. If it carries independent predictive content, it identifies the transition into dependence rather than the condition itself, which is a distinct economic event and a natural complement to Signal 1.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ind_zscore( winsor( delta( log( ratio( add( add( capx, aqc ), add( dlc, dvc ) ), add( che, ppent ) ) ), 1 ), 1 ) )
